questions.prompt: Why is a diode-connected MOSFET always in saturation when it conducts?
options: Its current is set by a source
Its drain is at the supply
questions.explanation: Gate and drain are the same node, so the saturation condition \(V_{DS} \ge V_{GS} - V_T\) reduces to \(V_T \ge 0\) (reader Sec. 13.3.1).

questions.prompt: A diode-connected NMOS has \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\) and \(r_o = 50\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). What small-signal resistance (Ω) does it present?
questions.explanation: A test voltage \(v\) gives \(v_{gs} = v\), so the controlled source draws \(g_mv\) like a conductance, in parallel with \(r_o\): \(1/(2.02\ \mathrm{mS}) = 495\ \Omega\). \(1/g_m\) alone is 500 Ω, a fine approximation.

questions.prompt: A diode-connected NMOS with \(\mu_nC_{ox}W/L = 2\ \mathrm{mA/V^2}\) and \(V_T = 0.45\ \mathrm{V}\) is fed \(I_B = 100\ \mu\mathrm{A}\). Find its DC voltage \(V_{GS}\) in V.
questions.explanation: \(V_{ov} = \sqrt{2(100\ \mu\mathrm{A})/(2\ \mathrm{mA/V^2})} = 0.316\ \mathrm{V}\), so \(V_{GS} = 0.766\ \mathrm{V}\). The device sets whatever \(V_{GS}\) carries the forced current.

questions.prompt: At fixed \(I_B\), you make the diode-connected device four times wider. What happens?
options: \(V_{GS}\) falls toward \(V_T\) and the impedance \(1/g_m\) halves
questions.explanation: \(V_{ov} \propto 1/\sqrt{W}\) at fixed current and \(g_m = \sqrt{2\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)I_B}\) doubles, so \(1/g_m\) halves.

questions.prompt: A diode-connected NMOS with \(\mu_nC_{ox}W/L = 1\ \mathrm{mA/V^2}\) carries \(50\ \mu\mathrm{A}\). Find its small-signal resistance \(1/g_m\) in kΩ (ignore \(r_o\)).
questions.explanation: \(g_m = \sqrt{2(1\ \mathrm{mA/V^2})(50\ \mu\mathrm{A})} = 0.316\ \mathrm{mS}\), so \(1/g_m = 3.16\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Low currents make diode loads large.

questions.prompt: A PMOS has its source at \(V_{DD}\) and its gate tied to its drain. What does it look like at the drain node, small-signal?
options: A resistance of about \(1/g_m\) to AC ground
questions.explanation: Same argument as NMOS: \(v_{sg} = -v\) at the drain, so the source current changes by \(g_mv\) in the direction that opposes \(v\). Only the polarity bookkeeping differs.

questions.prompt: A diode-connected NMOS has its drain and gate at the supply (AC ground) and its source as the output node; its body is grounded. With \(g_m = 1\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(g_{mb} = 0.2\ \mathrm{mS}\) and \(r_o\) ignored, what resistance (Ω) is seen at the source? (The body effect is a labelled prerequisite.)
questions.explanation: A test voltage at the source makes \(v_{gs} = v_{bs} = -v\), so the device draws \((g_m + g_{mb})v\): \(1/(1.2\ \mathrm{mS}) = 833\ \Omega\). Ignoring \(g_{mb}\) gives 1 kΩ.

questions.prompt: At fixed size, you double the bias current of a diode-connected device. How does its small-signal resistance change?
options: It falls by a factor of \(\sqrt2\)
questions.explanation: \(g_m \propto \sqrt{I}\) at fixed \(W/L\), so \(1/g_m\) drops by \(\sqrt2\). Halving assumes fixed \(V_{ov}\).

questions.prompt: Preview of the current mirror: a second NMOS shares the diode-connected device's gate and source. What sets its drain current?
options: The same \(V_{GS}\), so it copies the reference current, scaled by its \(W/L\)
questions.explanation: The diode device converts the current to a voltage; the second device converts it back.

questions.prompt: Preview of cascode sources: two diode-connected devices are stacked, one on top of the other, carrying the same current. What voltage appears at the top?
options: About \(2V_{GS}\), a convenient bias for the cascode device's gate
questions.explanation: Each diode drops one \(V_{GS}\). That level keeps both stacked devices of a cascode source in saturation with matched bias.
